docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
xlpro aims to be as similar to plain Python development as possible, such that the user isn't bound by a proprietary codebase. However, the quirks of integrating function calling and visualisation within Excel require some compromises which have to strike a balance of convenience, readability, performance and syntax.

As a result, there are some behaviours worth noting to the user, which we hope only require minor adjustments.

docs.title: Overview of Behaviours
docs.text:
1. String values stored in the Excel cells embed information.

    • "PyObj<...>" is a reference to an arbitrary Python object.
    • "Promise<...>" indicates that a cell is awaiting a return value from the server.
    • "...Exception(...)" or "...Error(...)" or any string representation of a Python exception indicates the Python function call raised an Exception, and you should debug the file.

  2. xlpro can handle showing simple, array or image types.

    • Basic types, str, float, int, bool.
    • Numpy types, np.float64, np.int32 and others.
    • Datetime types np.DateTime, these are cast from and to Excel serial representation if formatted to Date in Excel.
    • numpy.ndarray and pandas.Dataframe structures including the above dtypes can be shown in Excel.
    • Images and matplotlib figures are supported with the show_image() method.

  3. All input arrays or values are checked for the string "pyNone" (Excel name =pyNone), which is replaced by Python None. This will cast numpy arrays to dtype=object.

  4. Types are cast using PEP 484 type hinting. E.g. a 2D Excel array is cast to a xlpro.ndarray1d, xlpro.ndarray1d[np.float64], or list1d to maintain behaviour between row or column vector inputs.

  5. Python functions with optional arguments are supported. Providing no input, or explcitly using the =pyEmpty Excel Name will use the default arguments.

  6. For convenience and to minimise disruption, A simple undo/redo mechanism is built into xlpro to mitigate xlpro wiping Excel's undo stack. The undo-tracker is queried periodically to ensure it is active in order to avoid mishaps (should the VBA context crash or reset).

  7. For convenience, lists or tuples of objects are returned as column vector spill arrays natively. Use xlpro.condense() around the return type if you wish to enforce the result does not expand.

docs.title: Type Pre-Processing and Casting
docs.text:
xlpro wraps each function call coming from Excel with a type caster which is based on the type hints provided by the author in the function signature.

In its simplest form, this is necessary to cast the 2D array structure from Excel into predictable Python structures, not to mention the convenience of not needing to handle this in your function.

Note

If you want a function to be agnostic of a column or row vector in Excel, use a 1D data type hint, If you want to maintain the structure, use a 2D type hint.

The following built in types are provided as simple wrappers of the numpy.ndarray and list types.

from xlpro import (
    ndarray1d,
    ndarray2d,
    list1d,
    list2d,
)

EXPERIMENTAL - Complex casting

Numpy types will attempt to cast to xlpro.ndarray1d[np.float64] if provided as a type hint in the Python function signature, but this is experimental. If this doesn't give the desired behaviour, you could just use the xlpro.ndarray1d and cast using .astype(np.float64) at the beginning of your function.

def xl_array_to_npfloat64(arr:ndarray2d[np.float64])
    return arr # shape: (n, m), type: np.ndarray, dtype=np.float64

def xl_vector_to_npint32(arr:ndarray1d[np.int32])
    return arr # shape: (n,), type: np.ndarray, dtype=np.int32

docs.title: Empty Cell Handling
docs.text:
The communication pipeline between Excel and Python is expensive. Some tricks are used to prevent this from being flooded unnecessarily.

xlpro generally completes an isReady check on all function inputs to prevent wasted calls. On inputs up to 32 cells in size, if any of the input values are strictly empty Excel cells, the function call assumes it is waiting for the cell to be populated from a spill array, for example. Strictly empty cells would pass an ISBLANK() check, but may be a null string ="".

The scenarios where isReady = False are as follows:

  1. The argument is a Promise (indicating the cell is waiting for the result).
  2. The argument looks like a Python Exception .
  3. The argument is an Excel error value.
  4. The argument is an empty cell.

Passing None from Excel to Python

Want to deliberately pass None to Python? - use the =pyNone formula in the cells in question. This string is converted to Python None in the backend.

A note on casting when using None

The use of None has implications on xlpro's type casting argument pre-processor.

The use of None in your formulas will not affect casts to xlpro.list1d or xlpro.list2d, but casts to xlpro.ndarray1d or xlpro.ndarray2d will cause the numpy array to convert to dtype=object. If this is undesired, handle the conversion back in the first line of your function body. See XXX

For arrays larger than 32 cells, Numpy's behaviour is natural and empty cells will cast to NaN for numeric arrays.

Why do this?

Excel issues ghost function calls on any intermediate calculation, e.g. a subfunction of a larger formula. These flood the calculation queue and hog resources. Removing these while still in VBA-land is cheap, and significantly improves the performance of xlpro's calculation cycle.

docs.title: The Excel Undo Stack
docs.text:
xlpro is fundamentally a macro, and like any Excel macro which modifies the Workbook, any remote calls from the server which modify a cell immediately wipe the undo history of the workbook. This could mean that touching any input cell could immediately prevent you undoing your last command.

This behaviour is frankly always going to be dealbreaker for the user no matter how good the tool is otherwise. To mitigate the worst offending cases of this, xlpro includes a custom undo/redo mechanism which can handle basic cell formula changes, copy/pasting, and cut/pasting. This is intended to catch the case where you mistype over a cell which issues an xlpro-recalculation cycle and would otherwise be lost permanently.

If you plan on bulk changes, consider disabling automatic calculation.

Not all is lost

The native Excel undo stack is maintained where possible. Only by triggering a new/unique function call will the stack be wiped

VBA and Undo, a Very Common Problem

Managing the undo stack when dealing with VBA macros is a widely recognised limitation of Excel. xlpro's implementation is not perfect, but is effective if the sequence of selecting, typing, copying and pasting is kept simple. The hope is that this catches any small errors.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
xlpro writes data to the VSCode workspace to configure debugging using the Python Debugger extension provided by Microsoft. You probably already have this installed.

xlpro therefore supports breakpoints and raised exceptions as with any usual debugging process.

docs.title: Launching the Debugger
docs.text: Simply launch the Run and Debug > xlpro debugpy debugger to hook onto the running calculation server and hit breakpoints and exceptions. Note the recommended settings below.

docs.title: Debugging Recommended Settings
docs.text:
1. Command Pallette > Python: Clear Workspace Interepreter Setting
  2. Enables intellisense, syntax highlighting and code completion
  3. New terminals will activate the xlpro virtual environment by default
  4. Enable Uncaught Exceptions and User Uncaught Exceptions to catch ImportErrors and SyntaxErrors in your Python code.

docs.title: The Ribbon
docs.text:
After successful installation, the xlpro ribbon will appear in Excel. The ribbon is used to control the xlpro desktop application and the main interface for the end-user.

The primary workflow for xlpro from Excel is:

  1. Initialize (or reinitialize) the workbook.
  2. Start the calculation server.
  3. Sync your code to the server when it changes.
  4. Develop (and debug) the code in VSCode.
  5. Push your environment configuration to the server.
  6. Distribute your project.

docs.title: Initialize
docs.text:
Pressing the Initialize button opens a prompt to configure the initalization. This achieves one of the following:

  1. Configures the active workbook as a new xlpro project.
  2. Configures a matching Python environment for a pre-configured project.

Info

This spawns a console window which lets you configure the Python interpreter and will install any required packages. When re-initializing an existing project, you should match the Python version (you cannot accidentally use the wrong version) and say yes when prompted to install any additional dependencies (otherwise the project won't run!)

docs.title: Start
docs.text:
Pressing the Start button will start a new xlpro Python calculation server for the active initialized workbook. This server process handles all function and subroutine requests coming from Excel, and is tied to the workbook.

Use this for the following:

  • To start the project
  • If your Python environment/dependencies change, e.g. you ran pip install
  • If you need a hard reset of the calculation server, e.g. server crash

Manual Sync

The Start action attempts to also Sync. Sometimes this step is skipped in the case where Excel is inaccessible, e.g. locked in a dialogue. You may need to manually sync.

Restarting will Close any Running Server

Pressing Start will close any equivalent, live process, so you don't need to worry about closing the previous instance before restarting.

docs.title: Sync
docs.text:
Pressing the Sync button performs a soft-reset of an already running calculation server. Use this button to wipe the calculation cache or to re-load your Python files.

Use this for the following:

  • Your source files change, e.g. you register a new function in functions.py.
  • You want to clear all cached values.
  • The Start sequence did not trigger its internal Sync call (rare).

docs.title: Develop
docs.text:
Pressing the Develop button will open the xlpro project folder in VSCode.

Debugging Support

Note that VSCode debugging is supported natively, see the Debugging Guide for more information.

docs.title: Push Requirements
docs.text:
The Push Requirements button pushes the current state (requirements.txt, .python-version) of the project's Python interpreter to the *.xlpro folder.

If you are unfamiliar with Python, these two files essentially define the recipe which xlpro will read to Initialize an exactly matching environment.

Note

For example if you pip install a package, you would want to push the new interpreter state to reflect the necessary dependencies to run the project.

docs.title: Distribution
docs.text:
xlpro operates by placing all code and configuration files in an adjacent folder to the workbook. E.g. Book1.xlsx will have a Book1.xlsx.xlpro/ folder.

This *.xlpro folder contains all the necessary information for someone else to recreate your Python environment in one click. Simply share the workbook and folder together, e.g. in a .zip file, and someone else can replicate your project exactly.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
xlpro's desktop application configuration is stored in a config.toml file in the installation directory. There are a few options here, but the only critical one is VSCODE_PATH, which specifies how the Develop button can open VSCode for you to write your code.

If you haven't already configured your VSCODE_PATH, refer to the Hello World (Step-by-Step) video example video walkthrough, just note you may need to find the path to VSCode on your machine.

Configuration settings can be found in the drop-down shown. Press the Edit Global Config button in the Excel ribbon to open the config.toml file.

docs.title: Visual Studio Code Path Configuration
docs.text:
If the user has not added code.exe to PATH, you will see an error window when pressing the Develop button.It is necessary to manually point xlpro to the VSCode executable (generally Code.exe) in the config.

.xlpro/config.toml
# Default (assumes code.exe is in your PATH)
VSCODE_PATH = "code.exe"

# Custom (use this if the above is not configured in your PATH)
VSCODE_PATH = "path/to/code.exe" 
VSCODE_PATH = "path\\to\\code.exe" # Escaped backslashes

Where is code.exe?

Navigate to the 'Visual Studio Code' shortcut, probably via the start menu or desktop, and Right-Click > (Open File Location) > Properties > Target to show the path. Copy this and paste into config.toml.

The path depends on how VSCode was installed, but typically looks like one of the following:

C:\Users\Daniel Evans\AppData\Local\Programs\Microsoft VS Code\Code.exe
C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft VS Code\Code.exe

Escaped Characters

Like most formats, the toml file type uses the backslash \ character for escape sequences. When copying a path from Windows, you will need to replace all of the \ path separators with \\ or / for the file to parse correctly.

docs.title: Trust Access to the VBA Object Model
docs.text:
xlpro dynamically generates VBA code which accesses Python functions custom functions. This requires access to the VBA Object Model to add the generated code on the fly.

Follow these steps to trust VBA model access.

  1. Start Excel
  2. Open a workbook
  3. Click File > Options
  4. Navigate to the Trust Center tab
  5. Click Trust Center Settings...
  6. Navigate to the Macro Settings tab
  7. Check the box Trust access to the VBA project object model

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
xlpro comes with curated example projects.

You can navigate to the examples folder from Excel via the ribbon by clicking Manage xlpro > Show /.xlpro and navigating to the .xlpro/xlpro_examples folder.

  1. Open the preconfigured project Book1.xlsx.
  2. Initialize the project using the Initialize ribbon button
  3. Follow the default prompts to create a Python 3.13 environment with the (recommended) Create New Python 3.13 Environment option.
  4. Once the dependencies are installed, you can close the window
  5. Click Start to start the calculation server. Wait a few seconds for the registration to finish.
  6. Select a cell in the workbook and press F9 to recalculate the entire workbook.

docs.title: FAQs
docs.text:
Adding a FAQ section to crudely explain the functionality.

  1. Where is my Python server?

    • The xlpro application creates an isolated virtual environment from xlpro_init. This has its own installed dependencies, and these dependencies are written to the ./*.xlpro/ directory so the environment associated with a workbook can be reproduced.

  2. Can I have multiple workbooks active simultaneously?

    • Yes, workbook background servers are independent.

  3. Why don't recalculates enter my function breakpoints

    • xlpro fundamentally relies on a results cache to keep Excel's main thread free and responsive so Python can work in the background and send its results over when ready.
    • So, if xlpro has already calculated the results of a set of arguments, it will assume the existing calculation is valid (which may not be true if your Python code depends on a random number generator).
    • This cache is cleared when xlpro_refresh is called, so if you want to forcibly recalculate, consider refreshing first.
    • The cache is tagged with a uid based on the caller address, function name and arguments as values, so if the input values change, a recalculate will always be issued.

  4. How does debugging work?

    • xlpro uses the VSCode debugpy module to open a debug server at an available port. Once the server is running, this port is written into ./*.xlpro/.vscode/launch.json each time the server is created, so your debug configuration is updated as needed.

  5. How are dependencies managed?

    • xlpro uses uv to manage dependencies and Python versions. All of your virtual environments are kept within the installation directory /.xlpro/envs/ and a map between the workbooks

  6. xlpro is using a lot of space, how can I reduce it?

    • xlpro will create unique environments as requested by the user, each of these will likely include fully copies of the usual libraries such as matplotlib and numpy for example. This can consume a lot of storage if left unchecked.
    • xlpro supports linking many workbooks to one environment. Consider reusing a standard environment to prevent file duplication.
    • Want to clear the wasted space? Just delete the envs under .xlpro/envs/*. The next time you initialize a workbook xlpro will use the metadata kept with the workbook to create a fresh environment that matches the previous.

  7. Can I reuse a virtual environment for multiple workbooks?

    • Yes, In the xlpro_init dialogue when initializing a workbook, select an existing interpreter for another workbook. This will reduce the size of the xlpro installation directory.

  8. Can I configure a virtual environment somewhere else?

    • Yes, xlpro supports custom virtual environment paths. The xlpro application creates a symbolic link to this environment so it looks the same internally. This environment will need to be modified to install the xlpro Python module and its dependencies.
    • These symlinked environments must be virtual, and cannot be installation-level interpreters. We don't want to modify your system interpreter environment!

  9. Can I configure a standard python version and dependencies for my colleagues?

    • Pending development...
    • Some light modifications to the code can be made to support a default .python-version and requirements.txt on initialization.

  10. What if I lose my local data?

    • No worries! xlpro pushes the latest requirements of the virtual environment to the directory adjacent to the Excel workbook. So as long as you keep the workbook file and the .xlpro folder, you can always recreate your environment.
    • Store your workbooks on a server

  11. Sharing workbooks

    • As you might've read above, xlpro pushes the data needed to recreate the author's Python environment to the xlpro folder. Ship the workbook and xlpro folder together, and others can recreate your configuration in a few clicks.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
xlpro is designed to be installed at the user level. No admin rights necessary. Check if you meet the following requirements:

  1. Windows 10/11.
  2. Excel 365 or Excel 2021+.
  3. Visual Studio Code is installed (for development only).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
xlpro installs at the user level without the need for admin permissions. Where you need to perform the following steps to properly configure xlpro for your system.

You can find a walkthrough video in Hello World (Step by Step),

  1. Download and run the installer.
  2. Open Excel and you will see the xlpro ribbon is installed.
  3. Confirm the access to the VBA Object model is enabled.
  4. Confirm the configuration of VSCODE_PATH is correct.

That's all you need. Python can be installed on the fly. Refer to the video walkthroughs below for a step-by-step guide

docs.title: My Background
docs.text:
Hi, I'm Daniel, a mechanical engineer by training and programmer by passion. My time in industry has revealed that even world of engineering is bogged down in documentation, catching mistakes and time spent on readily-automatable processes.

I believe in the power of small-scale automation.

From the small business owner who needs to compile records, to the poorly engineer bound by ISO 13485 medical device quality management systems, I believe these small cases for automation are the last-mile delivery equivalent of the software industry - existing tools are too bespoke or costly, so everyone is still walking their Uber Eats orders 10-miles home on foot, so to speak.

Context switching is well-known cause of wasted time and mental fatigue. Time savings should not always be calculated by asking:

"How long would it take you to do X?"

but rather:

"How much time will we lose to context switching, validation, corrections and review loops if I let you do this manually?".

After learning to code in Python gradually over the past few years, I realised that most of what I actually spend my time doing in the office could be automated fairly easily, and I could be spending my time adding genuine value to the business.

But I'm hardly ever limited by the length of time it takes to write (... copy/paste from ChatGPT, come on) a 100-line Python script, it is fundamentally limited by distribution of code to an audience of colleagues. An audience which has at most a single-digit uptake in Python, but a 100% uptake in Excel.

What a convenient conclusion.

docs.title: Product Vision
docs.text:
What if Python could replace the functionality of VBA and more?

Excel is the most ubiquitous software on the planet. Estimates of the userbase reach as high as 1.5 billion, and millions daily-drive the software to make a living. From financial analysts to small business to data-entry, it seems there are millions of users who could leverage the power Python to increase quality, efficiency and robustness.

Compared to Excel, Python trades complexity for flexibility. You can write nearly any appliction, function, or automation in Python. This begs the question:

What if Python developers could seamlessly deploy code for the largest single pool of software users in the world?

Microsoft itself sees the value - having partnered with Anaconda to bake in a cloud version of Python support. This is a somewhat compelling option, but unsurprisingly looks like another 'cloud-native' data farm to sell compute credits to enterprise.

There is a simpler way - build a locally hosted Python calculation server accessible from Excel, support industry-standard IDEs, and let the community handle the rest.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
This tutorial shows how to build this workbook, which showcases some of the core behaviour and capabilities of xlpro, including a dynamic figure which updates in real-time with the spreadsheet.

The figure pulls x, y, data in plain Excel and is generates a simple matplotlib figure.

docs.title: Initialize and Download Python
docs.text: Create a new workbook, initialize it in xlpro using the button, use the (recommended) Create New Python 3.13 Environment option. This will download a new interpreter and will prompt you to install the dependencies for pre-existing projects.

docs.title: Writing and Using a Function
docs.text:
Open the VSCode workspace using the Develop ribbon button.

Add the following code to functions.py in the VSCode workspace. When we run the server, we will find a matching function becomes registered in Excel.

import xlpro

def custom_adder(a, b):
    return a + b

Start the server in Excel by pressing the Start button. This will create a startup process which will close in a few seconds, and a child process which shows the running Python calculation server for the workbook.

After a few seconds, the server will have prepared the VBA UDFs. In Excel, enter =custom_adder(1, 2), you should see the result 3 appear in the cell. Use the Sync button to try again if the function does not exist (e.g. #NAME error indicating the function does not exist.).

Now point the function to reference some cells, e.g. =custom_adder(A1, A2). Ensure both inputs are explicitly given as values, i.e. not blank cells, we'll touch on this later.

docs.title: Returning Python Objects
docs.text:
Create a new function custom_adder_matrix. This function will take an 2D Excel argument a a, convert to a np.ndarray matrix, add b and return the result.

# Define a function which returns a matrix, this will return 
# a np.ndarray object
def custom_adder_matrix(a, b):
    a_mat = np.array(a)
    return a_mat + b

You will notice that the matrix equation returns a PyObj... value. This indicates the cell points to an object reference.

docs.title: Showing a PyObj
docs.text:
For now, we can use the xlpro.show() method and call it from Excel to visualise the result. Add this code to functions.py to register the show() function in Excel.

# Register 
xlpro.register(xlpro.show)

In Excel, use the formula =show(X) on the PyObj... cell. This will expand the result so you can pull the data into Excel for inspection, visualisation, or to pass to Excel functions or plots. Watch out to not create a #SPILL error.

Something similar can be done with figure or image objects.

docs.title: Optional Arguments
docs.text:
Optional arguments can be declared. Try the following function in Excel and toggle the flag on and off.

# Optional arguments
def adder_or_subtractor(a, b, do_add:bool=True):
    if do_add:
       return a + b
    return a - b

docs.text: Complex function inputs can be difficult to provide correctly in Excel. Use Excel's formula helper to

docs.title: Arrays and Type Casting
docs.text:
In Excel, all range values are given as a row-major array. I.e. rows are returned as a 1 by m 2D array, and columns are returned as a n by 1 2D array. This would require the user to handle either case which could be cumbersome. xlpro features basic array type casting so you can choose whether to preserve the 2D shape of the input.

Create two new functions and import the classes needed for PEP 484 type hints.

# Import types for implicit casting
from xlpro import list1d, list2d, ndarray1d, ndarray2d

def custom_adder_matrix(matrix:ndarray2d, constant:float):
    return matrix + constant

def custom_adder_always_vector(vector:ndarray1d, constant:float):
    return vector + constant

Try the following cases and inspect the output using =show() in Excel.

  1. Try custom_adder_matrix(matrix, constant) with a ...
    1. (n x m) matrix (shape is maintained)
    2. (n x 1) matrix (row vector maintained)
    3. (1 x m) matrix (column vector maintained)
  2. Try custom_adder_always_vector(vector, constant) with a ...
    1. (n x 1) vector (returns n by 1 column vector)
    2. (1 x m) vector (returns m by 1 column vector)
    3. (n x m) vector (Exception, ndarray1d does not support 2D data types)

The companion types list1d and list2d behave similarly.

docs.title: Creating a Figure
docs.text:
A matplotlib figure is a great tool for visualising data. We can write a function which takes three inputs xdata, ydata, and a linelabel to create a figure with a labelled line.

Prepare the file for using matplotlib figures like so:

# Import matplotlib and configure it to use a non-gui backend
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Then you can create a function which returns a matplotlib.figure.Figure, which we can use later in Excel.

def create_matplotlib_figure(
    xdata:ndarray1d, # cast to a 1D array for convenience
    ydata:ndarray1d, # as above
    linelabel:str="", # the label of the line
    create_legend:bool=False # boolean flag to create legend
):
    """Function which takes x and y data and generates a matplotlib figure, 
    and labels the line in the legend. Gives the user basic options to 
    configure a legend
    """

    # Create the figure
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()

    # Plot the data and retrieve the line handle to use in the legend
    ln, = ax.plot(xdata, ydata)

    # Add axes labels
    ax.set_xlabel("x-values")
    ax.set_ylabel("y-values")

    # Add a legend if the flag is provided
    if create_legend:
       ax.legend([ln], [linelabel], frameon=False)

    # resize the figure to 170 by 100 mm.
    fig.set_size_inches(np.array((170, 100)) / 25.4)

    return fig # type: matplotlib.figure.Figure

Now in Excel, create some data for the x and y vectors in Excel and try the create_matplotlib_figure function. Ensure each input is a fully populated explocit array (i.e. no blank cells.)

When you see a PyObj output of this cell, it is ready to show using the show_image() function.

docs.title: Showing a Figure Object
docs.text:
Register the xlpro.show_image function in Excel via the following:

# functions.py
xlpro.register()(xlpro.show_image) # registers '=show_image()' in Excel

The show_image function takes the following form:

  • excel_image_id: the unique string id of the image in Excel
  • obj: the figure object to show
  • seed: an argument purely to prompt recalculate.
show_image(excel_image_id:'str', figure:'Figure', seed:'Any'=None):

Sync from Excel to update the function register. Call =show_image(...), providing the required excel_image_id and figure values. You will see a figure be added to Excel nearby. Note that seed is not required in this case, but you can use it to bump updates. You can also use the Recalculate Selected ribbon button.

Note the name of the figure in Excel will match the argument.

docs.title: Dynamic Figure Updates and seed
docs.text:
It is possible to sequentially add lines to a figure object by applying a function which performs a change to the figure, e.g. add_line_to_axes(xdata, ydata, lineformat). The issue this raises is the timing of a show_image() call in Excel. We will end up with a race condition where the figure may not reflect the latest changes.

To manage this, the seed argument is intended to be any value which drives the render step. If this value is driven by all of the cells which manipulate the figure, then the show_image() function will only execute when the precedents have completed successfully.

docs.title: Debugging Example
docs.text:
Copy-paste this function below into your project and call it from Excel. You will get a KeyError('Banana') return in Excel.

# functions.py
def get_banana_price():
    """Function which simulates fetching price data from an external source,
    and returns the price of bananas. 
    """
    key = "Banana"
    price_cents_per_kg = {
        "Apple":     99,
        "Orange":    140,
        "banana":    87, # hint...
        "Kiwi":      180,
        "Mango":     204,
        "Pineapple": 316,
    }
    return price_cents_per_kg[key]

Sync and try out the function in Excel. We get a KeyError response in the cell.

Now try out the debugger in VSCode, we will connect to the calculation server, so ensure the calculation server (Start button) is still running.

  1. Add a breakpoint on the return price_cents_per_kg[key] line in VSCode
  2. Navigate to the Run and Debug pane (ctrl + shift + D)
  3. Run the xlpro debugpy debug configuration to connect.

Re-run the calculation by either:

  • Sync-ing and recalculating the workbook e.g. using F9
  • Calling get_banana_price() from a new cell

The breakpoint should hit. If you are new to Python debugging, take note of:

  1. The highlighted area showing the next line to be executed
  2. The Variables explorer area in the top-left
  3. The Debug Console at the bottom can be used to evaluate debugging code.

You can see that the error was caused by a case-mismatch in the strings all along...

Debugger Settings

Activating the Raised Exceptions flag in the bottom left corner of VSCode will cause the debugger to break on all exceptions.

E.g. with our previous example we will see this.

A Note On Breakpoints, and Excel Hangs

When you hit a breakpoint the entire calculation server pauses. This can cause the Excel UI to become unresponsive as it is unable to get a response from the calculation server.

This is simply caused by the entire Python process pausing when a breakpoint is hit, so resuming the server (or closing it) will let Excel resume.

docs.title: Installing a Package
docs.text:
You may want to install packages to develop a more complex project beyond matplotlib, pandas and numpy. Lets install the yfinance package and build a graph to visualise some financial data.

This is as simple as opening a terminal in VSCode, and running pip install ...

Info

Ensure you run the Python: Clear Workspace Interpreter Setting from the command pallette (ctrl + shift + P) so VSCode knows which interpreter to activate.

Why? - xlpro relies on the Python exe path written to .vscode/settings.json.

Now create a new terminal using ctrl + shift + ' or Terminal > New.

VSCode should pull the correct setting and automatically activate the correct environment. Now pip will install to the right Python interpreter.

Reminder

If you install a new requirement, you should remember to also Push Requirements from the xlpro Excel ribbon to keep the server files up to date.

docs.title: Using annotations
docs.text:
Annotations consist of two parts: a marker, which can be placed anywhere in a block marked with the annotate class, and content located in a list below the block containing the marker:

Text with annotations
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, (1) consectetur adipiscing elit.
{ .annotate }

1.  :man_raising_hand: I'm an annotation! I can contain `code`, __formatted
    text__, images, ... basically anything that can be expressed in Markdown.

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, (1) consectetur adipiscing elit.

  1. I'm an annotation! I can contain code, formatted text, images, ... basically anything that can be written in Markdown.

Note that the annotate class must only be added to the outermost block. All nested elements can use the same list to define annotations, except when annotations are nested themselves.

docs.title: in annotations
docs.text:
When SuperFences is enabled, annotations can be nested inside annotations by adding the annotate class to the list item hosting the annotation content, repeating the process:

Text with nested annotations

{ .annotate }

1.  :man_raising_hand: I'm an annotation! (1)
    { .annotate }

    1.  :woman_raising_hand: I'm an annotation as well!

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, (1) consectetur adipiscing elit.

  1. I'm an annotation! (1)

    1. I'm an annotation as well!

docs.text:
The titles and bodies of admonitions can also host annotations by adding the annotate modifier after the type qualifier, which is similar to how inline blocks work:

    euismod nulla. Curabitur feugiat, tortor non consequat finibus, justo

docs.title: in everything else
docs.text:
The Attribute Lists extension is the key ingredient for adding annotations to most elements, but it has some limitations. However, it's always possible to leverage the Markdown in HTML extension to wrap arbitrary elements with a div with the annotate class:

HTML with annotations
<div class="annotate" markdown>

> Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, (1) consectetur adipiscing elit.

</div>

1.  :man_raising_hand: I'm an annotation!

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, (1) consectetur adipiscing elit.

  1. I'm an annotation!

With this trick, annotations can also be added to blockquotes, lists, and many other elements that are not supported by the Attribute Lists extension. Furthermore, note that code blocks follow different semantics.

Known limitations

Please note that annotations currently don't work in data tables as reported in #3453, as data tables are scrollable elements and positioning is very tricky to get right. This might be fixed in the future.

docs.text:
1. Install the Latest Release xlpro-v0.1.0-installer.exe or visit our download page for other releases

  2. Run the installer

  3. Configure the Excel Trust Center Settings within Excel to trust access to the VBA project model.

All done! Open up a workbook and you should see the xlpro ribbon in Excel

docs.title: Enable Trust Access to the VBA Object Model
docs.text:
xlpro currently uses dynamically allocated VBA modules to register UDFs while the background Python server is running. This requires access to the VBA object model, which can expose your machine to attacks

  1. Start Excel
  2. Open a workbook
  3. Click File > Options
  4. Navigate to the Trust Center tab
  5. Click Trust Center Settings...
  6. Navigate to the Macro Settings tab
  7. Check the box Trust access to the VBA project object model

Update Pending

xlpro will soon not require access the VBA object model. Once complete, this can be revoked.

docs.title: Quick-Start
docs.text: First time user? Open the example workbook c:/users/<USERNAME>/.xlpro/examples/xlpro_example1.xlsx

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text:
Click the xlpro_init ribbon button. This will prompt you to configure a python installation >=3.8. Select the recommended option to install the our recommended python version python 3.13.

The workbook is now ready to run code. xlpro has created a /book1.xlsx.xlpro folder next to book1.xlsx ready to be used in VSCode.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: Click the start_vscode ribbon button to open up the ./book1.xlsx.xlpro/ directory in VSCode (or you can do this manually).

docs.title: User Defined Functions
docs.text: Write any functions in functions.py that you wish to be accessible as User Defined Functions (UDFs) in Excel.

docs.title: Run the Server
docs.text:
xlpro deploys a background python server (based on whichever was selected above) which has two functions:

  1. Executing your Python code
  2. Updating/registering the Excel UDFs

Click the xlpro_start to start the server - this will start a shell window which is the python process. As long as this window is running, the Python server is running.

docs.title: Reload Functions
docs.text:
Click the xlpro_refresh ribbon button to load/reload your functions into Excel. You can now issue a worksheet recalculate.

Asynchronous Execution

xlpro executes the code in a separate thread to Excel, so it has nearly no impact on Excel's responsiveness. You will likely see a placeholder string value appear before you see your function outputs because of this!

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
xlpro configures the vscode debugging task to hook onto the running Python background server. In your vscode project for the workbook, navigate to the Run and Debug pane and run the xlpro debugpy while the background server is running.

Add a breakpoint to a function being used in Excel - then click refresh and recalculate. You should have entered a breakpoint which you can use for debugging. Note this will pause the background python server.

Debugging

IDE debuggers are a great way to debug python code. We recommend entering a breakpoint, and using the variable explorer and debug console to test your code.

docs.title: FAQs
docs.text:
Adding a FAQ section to explain

  1. Where is my Python server?

    • The xlpro application creates an isolated virtual environment from xlpro_init. This has its own installed dependencies, and these dependencies are written to the ./*.xlpro/ directory so they can always be

  2. Can I have multiple workbooks active simultaneously?

    • Yes, workbook background servers are independent.

  3. Why don't recalculates enter my function breakpoints

    • xlpro fundamentally relies on a results cache to keep Excel's main thread free and responsive so Python can work in the background and send its results over when ready.
    • This cache is cleared when xlpro_refresh is called, so if you want to forcibly recalculate, consider refreshing first.
    • The cache is tagged with a uid based on the caller address, function name and arguments as values, so if the input values change, a recalculate will be issued. This may be desireable in some cases.

  4. How does debugging work?

    • xlpro uses the VSCode debugpy module to open a debug server at a specific port. This port is written into ./*.xlpro/.vscode/launch.json each time the server is created

  5. How are dependencies managed?

    • xlpro uses uv to manage dependencies and Python versions. All of your virtual environments are kept within the installation directory /.xlpro/envs/ and a map between the workbooks

  6. Can I reuse a virtual environment for multiple workbooks?

    • Yes, In the xlpro_init dialogue when initializing a workbook, select an existing interpreter for another workbook. This will reduce the size of the xlpro installation directory.
    • Note: This is a great way to reduce the

  7. Can I configure a virtual environment somewhere else?

    • Yes, xlpro supports custom virtual environment paths. The xlpro application creates a symbolic link to this environment so it looks the same internally. This environment will need to be modified to install the xlpro Python module and its dependencies.
    • symlinked environments must be virtual, and cannot be installation-level interpreters.

  8. Can I configure a standard python version and dependencies for my colleagues?

    • Pending development...
    • Some light modifications to the code can be made to support a default .python-version and requirements.txt on initialization.

  9. What if I lose my local virtual environment settings?

    • No worries! xlpro pushes the latest requirements of the virtual environment to the directory adjacent to the excel workbook. So as long as you keep the workbook file and the .xlpro folder, you can always recreate your environment.

xlpro requires access to the VBA editor to install the xlpro type library. Enable this in your Excel trust-centre options.

The xlpro add-in must be added to the XLSTART folder to ensure it is loaded when Excel starts.
